::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- draw **histograms** and **density plots** and explain how bin width and bandwidth change what you see;
- identify every element of a **boxplot** (quartiles, whiskers, outliers, notches) and interpret it correctly;
- use **violin plots**, **jittered points** and **ECDFs** to show distributions in more detail;
- choose a sensible plot to **compare a numeric variable across groups**.
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

## 1. Why plot a distribution?

In [Summary statistics](../05-descriptive/22-summary-statistics.qmd) we compressed a variable into a few numbers. Numbers alone can be badly misleading. The `faithful` data record `r nrow(faithful)` eruptions of the Old Faithful geyser; the mean eruption length is `r round(mean(faithful$eruptions), 2)` minutes. Is that a "typical" eruption?

```{r}
#| label: fig-faithful-intro
#| fig-cap: "Eruption durations of Old Faithful. The dashed line is the mean: almost no eruption lasts that long."
ggplot(faithful, aes(eruptions)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 1.5,
                 fill = "grey70", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(faithful$eruptions), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Eruption duration (minutes)", y = "Number of eruptions")
```

No. There are **two kinds** of eruptions — short ones of about 2 minutes and long ones of about 4–5 minutes — and the mean falls in the gap between them. A distribution with two peaks is called **bimodal**. Only a plot reveals this.

## 2. Histograms

A **histogram** is the picture of a frequency table of classes (see [Frequency tables](../05-descriptive/21-frequency-tables.qmd)): the x axis is divided into adjacent **bins** and the height of each bar is the number of observations in the bin. Unlike a bar chart, the bars touch, because the x axis is a continuous number line.

### Bins change the story

You control the bins with `bins` (how many) or, better, `binwidth` (how wide) and `boundary` (where one bin edge falls):

```{r}
#| label: fig-bins
#| fig-cap: "The same data with three bin widths."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "binwidth = 1.5: too wide"
#|   - "binwidth = 0.25: about right"
#|   - "binwidth = 0.02: too narrow"
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-asp: 0.9
h <- ggplot(faithful, aes(eruptions)) +
  labs(x = "Duration (min)", y = "Count")

h + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1.5, boundary = 1.5, colour = "white")
h + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, boundary = 1.5, colour = "white")
h + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02, boundary = 1.5, colour = "white")
```

- With **very wide bins** the two groups merge into one hump: the bimodality disappears.
- With **very narrow bins** each bar holds just a few eruptions and random noise dominates.
- In between, the main features are visible. Always try **several bin widths** before settling; ggplot2 uses 30 bins by default and prints a message asking you to choose a better value.

Choose `binwidth` in round units of the variable (0.25 minutes, 5 mm, 500 g) and set `boundary` so that bin edges fall on round numbers: readers can then read the bins.

### Counts or density?

By default the y axis shows **counts**. With `aes(y = after_stat(density))` it shows a **density**: bar *areas* add up to 1, so histograms of groups of different sizes become comparable and a density curve can be drawn on top:

```{r}
#| label: fig-hist-density
#| fig-cap: "Histogram on the density scale with a kernel density estimate on top."
ggplot(faithful, aes(eruptions)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 0.25,
                 boundary = 1.5, fill = "grey80", colour = "white") +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Eruption duration (minutes)", y = "Density")
```

`after_stat()` refers to a variable computed by the geom's statistic (here the density of each bin) rather than a column of the data.

## 3. Density plots

A **density plot** (kernel density estimate) is a smooth version of a histogram. Imagine putting a small bell-shaped "bump" on every observation and adding them up: where many observations are close together, the bumps pile up into a peak. The total area under the curve is 1, so the height is not a count but a *relative concentration* of observations.

The width of the bumps is the **bandwidth**; you scale it with `adjust` (default 1):

```{r}
#| label: fig-adjust
#| fig-cap: "The bandwidth plays the role of the bin width: too small shows noise, too large hides structure."
ggplot(faithful, aes(eruptions)) +
  geom_density(adjust = 0.25, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_density(adjust = 1, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_density(adjust = 3, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Eruption duration (minutes)", y = "Density",
       subtitle = "adjust = 0.25 (dotted), 1 (solid), 3 (dashed)")
```

Density plots are excellent for **comparing a few groups** on the same axes:

```{r}
#| label: fig-density-groups
#| fig-cap: "Body mass by species: transparent fills let all three curves remain visible."
ggplot(penguins, aes(body_mass, fill = species)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Density", fill = "Species")
```

Be aware that a density curve can extend beyond the possible range of the data (for example below zero for a positive variable) and can make very small samples look smoother than the evidence justifies.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the kernel density estimator

For data $x_1, \dots, x_n$, the kernel density estimate at a point $x$ is

$$
\hat f(x) = \frac{1}{n h} \sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x - x_i}{h}\right),
$$

where $K$ is a **kernel** (a symmetric density, by default the standard normal) and $h > 0$ is the **bandwidth**. ggplot2 uses `bw.nrd0()` (Silverman's rule of thumb), $h = 0.9 \min(s, \mathrm{IQR}/1.34)\, n^{-1/5}$, multiplied by `adjust`. For the eruptions:

```{r}
#| label: bandwidth
bw.nrd0(faithful$eruptions)
```

Base R's `density()` computes the same estimate.
:::

## 4. Boxplots: every element explained

A **boxplot** (Tukey's box-and-whisker plot) draws the five-number summary from [Summary statistics](../05-descriptive/22-summary-statistics.qmd) plus a rule for flagging unusual values. Let us compute each element for the ozone concentration in `airquality` and then see where it appears.

```{r}
#| label: box-elements
ozone <- airquality$Ozone[!is.na(airquality$Ozone)]

q <- quantile(ozone, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
iqr <- q[[3]] - q[[1]]
fences <- c(lower = q[[1]] - 1.5 * iqr, upper = q[[3]] + 1.5 * iqr)

q
fences
c(lower_whisker = min(ozone[ozone >= fences[["lower"]]]),
  upper_whisker = max(ozone[ozone <= fences[["upper"]]]))
ozone[ozone > fences[["upper"]] | ozone < fences[["lower"]]]
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-box-anatomy
#| fig-cap: "Anatomy of a boxplot, computed on the ozone data."
#| fig-asp: 0.45
labels_df <- tibble(
  x = c(q[[1]], q[[2]], q[[3]], max(ozone[ozone <= fences[["upper"]]]), 150),
  label = c("Q1", "median", "Q3", "end of\nwhisker", "outliers")
)

ggplot(tibble(ozone), aes(x = ozone, y = 0)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(group = 1), width = 0.3, orientation = "y") +
  geom_text(data = labels_df, aes(x = x, y = 0.25, label = label),
            size = 3.5, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.3, 0.35), breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Ozone (ppb)", y = NULL)
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read a boxplot

- **The box** goes from the first quartile (Q1 = `r q[[1]]`) to the third quartile (Q3 = `r q[[3]]`): it contains the **middle 50%** of the observations. Its length is the IQR (`r iqr`).
- **The line inside the box** is the **median** (`r q[[2]]`). Its position inside the box hints at skewness: here it is closer to Q1, and the right part of the box is longer — a right-skewed distribution.
- **The whiskers** extend from the box to the **most extreme observation that lies within 1.5 × IQR of the box**. They do *not* end exactly at Q3 + 1.5 × IQR (`r fences[["upper"]]`); here the upper whisker ends at the observed value `r max(ozone[ozone <= fences[["upper"]]])`. The lower whisker ends at the minimum (`r min(ozone)`) because no value is below the lower fence.
- **Points beyond the whiskers** are drawn individually as **potential outliers** (here `r paste(sort(ozone[ozone > fences[["upper"]]]), collapse = " and ")`). They are values worth checking, *not* automatically errors and *not* something to delete. In skewed data, many perfectly valid observations end up beyond the whiskers.
:::

The quartiles of `geom_boxplot()` are computed with `quantile()` (type 7). Base R's `boxplot()` uses Tukey's hinges (`fivenum()`), so the two can differ very slightly.

### What a boxplot hides

A boxplot shows five numbers and the outliers — nothing else. Two very different distributions can have the same boxplot. The bimodal eruptions look perfectly ordinary in a boxplot:

```{r}
#| label: fig-box-hides
#| fig-cap: "The boxplot of eruption durations gives no hint of the two clusters that the histogram showed so clearly."
#| fig-asp: 0.35
ggplot(faithful, aes(x = eruptions, y = "")) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Eruption duration (minutes)", y = NULL)
```

This is why boxplots are best **combined with the points** or used for quick comparisons of many groups whose shape you have already checked.

## 5. Comparing groups: ozone by month

The old version of this course explored New York ozone levels by month. We prepare the data first: `Month` becomes a factor with month names, and a new categorical variable splits each month into beginning, middle and end.

```{r}
#| label: air-data
air <- airquality |>
  filter(!is.na(Ozone)) |>
  mutate(
    Month = factor(Month, levels = 5:9, labels = month.name[5:9]),
    day_cat = case_when(
      Day < 10 ~ "Begin",
      Day < 20 ~ "Middle",
      .default = "End"
    ) |>
      factor(levels = c("Begin", "Middle", "End"))
  ) |>
  select(Ozone, Wind, Month, Day, day_cat)

count(air, Month)
```

Note that June has only `r sum(air$Month == "June")` days with an ozone measurement: keep this in mind when comparing.

```{r}
#| label: fig-air-box
#| fig-cap: "Ozone by month. Points: the monthly means added with stat_summary()."
box_air <- ggplot(air, aes(x = Month, y = Ozone)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Ozone (ppb)")

box_air +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = "#D55E00", outlier.shape = 17,
               outlier.size = 2.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3, colour = "#0072B2")
```

- The `outlier.*` arguments change how flagged points look.
- `stat_summary(fun = mean, ...)` computes a summary for each group and draws it (the old argument `fun.y` is deprecated: use `fun`).
- July and August have the highest ozone levels. In four of the five months the mean lies clearly above the median, a sign of right skew within months (in July the two are almost equal).

Variants of the same plot:

```{r}
#| label: fig-air-variants
#| fig-cap: "Two variants of the monthly boxplots."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Horizontal boxes with coord_flip()"
#|   - "Colour by month, legend removed"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-asp: 0.8
box_air + geom_boxplot() + coord_flip()

ggplot(air, aes(Month, Ozone, colour = Month)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  guides(colour = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Ozone (ppb)")
```

Removing the legend in the second plot is correct: month is already written on the axis, so the legend would be redundant ink. Colour adds no information here — use it only when it encodes something.

Boxplots for **two grouping variables** use `fill` (or `colour`) for the second one:

```{r}
#| label: fig-air-two-groups
#| fig-cap: "Ozone by month and by part of the month."
ggplot(air, aes(Month, Ozone, fill = day_cat)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Ozone (ppb)", fill = "Part of month")
```

With three boxes per month, most boxes summarise fewer than 10 days — the "End" box for June only one day: an attractive plot can be built on very little data.

## 6. Notched boxplots

A **notch** narrows the box around the median. Its half-width is

$$
1.58 \times \frac{\mathrm{IQR}}{\sqrt{n}} .
$$

```{r}
#| label: fig-notch
#| fig-cap: "Notched boxplots. In June (n = 9) the notch is wider than the box, so the box looks 'folded'."
box_air + geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read notches

- Notches are designed for **comparing medians** between boxes: if the notches of two boxes **do not overlap**, this is rough evidence (at about the 5% level) that the population medians differ. May and July are a clear example.
- **Overlapping** notches do *not* prove that medians are equal — just as a non-significant test does not prove "no difference".
- A notch is **not** a confidence interval for one median on its own, and it says nothing about means.
- With small groups the notch can extend beyond the box (June, `r sum(air$Month == "June")` days): the comparison is then very imprecise. ggplot2 warns about this.
- The formula assumes roughly symmetric data and independent observations; consecutive days of ozone are not really independent, so treat notches here as a visual hint. Formal comparisons are in [Non-parametric tests](../08-inference/36-nonparametric-tests.qmd).
:::

## 7. Showing the points: jitter and dot plots

With a few dozen observations per group, **show every observation**. Points at the same x position overlap; **jittering** adds a small random horizontal shift:

```{r}
#| label: fig-jitter
#| fig-cap: "Boxplots with the individual days. outlier.shape = NA avoids drawing the outliers twice."
box_air +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.6, colour = "#0072B2")
```

- `height = 0` is important: never jitter the variable you are measuring.
- Because the jitter layer already shows every point, `outlier.shape = NA` hides the boxplot's own outlier points (otherwise they would appear twice).
- Without jitter (`geom_point()`), values with the same ozone in the same month would be drawn on top of each other and hidden.

A **dot plot** stacks the points instead of scattering them:

```{r}
#| label: fig-dotplot
#| fig-cap: "Boxplots with a centred dot plot."
box_air +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center", dotsize = 0.6,
               binwidth = 4)
```

## 8. Violin plots

A **violin plot** draws a mirrored density curve for each group, so it shows the **shape** (including several peaks) that a boxplot hides. A narrow boxplot inside adds the quartiles:

```{r}
#| label: fig-violin
#| fig-cap: "Violin plots of penguin body mass by species, with narrow boxplots inside."
ggplot(penguins, aes(species, body_mass, fill = species)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, fill = "white", outlier.shape = NA,
               na.rm = TRUE) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Body mass (g)")
```

The width of the violin at a given height reflects how many penguins have that mass. Like density plots, violins can mislead with very small groups, so mention (or show) $n$.

## 9. Empirical cumulative distribution functions (ECDF)

The **ECDF** answers, for every value $x$: *what proportion of observations is less than or equal to $x$?* It is the plot of the cumulative relative frequencies, and it needs **no bins and no bandwidth** — every observation is used exactly as it is.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ecdf
#| fig-cap: "ECDF of body mass by species. Read the y value at a given mass as 'proportion of birds at most this heavy'."
ggplot(penguins, aes(body_mass, colour = species)) +
  stat_ecdf(linewidth = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 4000, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Proportion of birds ≤ x", colour = "Species")
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- At 4000 g (dashed line) the Adelie and Chinstrap curves are near 0.78: about `r round(100 * mean(penguins$body_mass[penguins$species == "Adelie"] <= 4000, na.rm = TRUE))`% of Adelie penguins weigh at most 4 kg; the Gentoo curve is still near 0 (`r round(100 * mean(penguins$body_mass[penguins$species == "Gentoo"] <= 4000, na.rm = TRUE))`%).
- Reading **horizontally** gives quantiles: where a curve crosses 0.5 is the median of that group.
- A curve further to the **right** means larger values. Steep parts are where many observations are concentrated; flat parts are gaps.
- Base R: `ecdf(x)` returns a function, e.g. `ecdf(penguins$body_mass)(4000)`.
:::

ECDFs are less intuitive than histograms at first, but they are the most honest way to compare whole distributions, and they reappear in tests (Kolmogorov–Smirnov) and simulations.

## 10. Choosing a plot for a numeric variable

| Goal | Good choice | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Shape of one variable | Histogram (try several bin widths), density | Bin width / bandwidth |
| Compare 2–4 groups in detail | Overlaid densities, violins + points, ECDFs | Small groups look smooth |
| Compare many groups quickly | Boxplots (+ jitter if few points) | Boxplots hide multimodality |
| Few observations (< ~30 per group) | Points (jitter or dot plot), possibly with a boxplot | Densities and violins over-smooth |
| Proportions below/above a value | ECDF | Less familiar to readers |

For many groups, a **ridgeline plot** (stacked density curves, from the `ggridges` package: `ggridges::geom_density_ridges()`) is another compact option.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Trusting the default 30 bins.** The number of bins can create or hide features. Try several, and pick round bin widths.
2. **Calling whisker ends "minimum and maximum".** They are the most extreme points *within 1.5 × IQR of the box*; points beyond are drawn separately.
3. **Deleting "outliers" because a boxplot flagged them.** The 1.5 × IQR rule is a screening tool, not a verdict; skewed data have many legitimate flagged values.
4. **Reading overlapping notches as "the medians are equal".** Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
5. **Jittering vertically** (`height` not set to 0) in a plot where the y axis is the measurement — you change the data.
6. **Drawing outliers twice** when combining `geom_boxplot()` with `geom_jitter()` (use `outlier.shape = NA`).
:::

## 11. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. In a boxplot the median line is close to the top of the box and the lower whisker is long. What does this suggest about the shape?

A **left-skewed** distribution: the lower half of the data is more spread out than the upper half.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. Two histograms of the same data look very different. How is that possible?

They use different bin widths (or bin boundaries). The data are the same; the grouping is not. That is why you should try several bin widths.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. On an ECDF plot, the curve for group A crosses 0.5 at 30 and the curve for group B at 45. What do you conclude?

The median of A is about 30 and the median of B about 45: values in B tend to be larger (its curve lies to the right).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q4. Why is a violin plot more informative than a boxplot for the `faithful` eruptions?

The violin shows the density, so the two peaks (short and long eruptions) are visible; the boxplot shows only quartiles, which hide the bimodality.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_25_1
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(faithful, aes(waiting)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = ______, boundary = 40, colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Waiting time (minutes)", y = "Count")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_25_1"}
Replace the blank with a number and run the code several times.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_25_1"}
```r
ggplot(faithful, aes(waiting)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 40, colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Waiting time (minutes)", y = "Count")
```
`binwidth = 5` shows clearly that the waiting times are **bimodal** (peaks around 50–55 and 75–85 minutes). With 20 minutes the shape is crude; with 1 minute it is noisy.
:::

[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — boxplot plus points.** Using `ToothGrowth`, draw boxplots of tooth length (`len`) for each dose, with jittered points on top and without duplicated outliers. Remember that `dose` is numeric.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_25_2
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(x = ______, y = len)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = ______) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = ______, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Dose (mg/day)", y = "Tooth length")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_25_2"}
Use `factor(dose)` on the x axis, `outlier.shape = NA` and `height = 0`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_25_2"}
```r
ggplot(ToothGrowth, aes(x = factor(dose), y = len)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Dose (mg/day)", y = "Tooth length")
```
Tooth length increases with the dose. Without `factor()`, ggplot2 would treat dose as continuous and draw a single box.
:::

[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — compute the whiskers.** Compute by hand where the whiskers of a boxplot of `mtcars$hp` end and which cars are flagged as outliers. Then check with a plot.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_25_3
x <- mtcars$hp
q <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75))
iqr <- ______
upper_fence <- q[[2]] + ______ * iqr
max(x[x <= upper_fence])           # end of the upper whisker
rownames(mtcars)[x > ______]       # flagged cars
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_25_3"}
`iqr <- q[[2]] - q[[1]]`, and the fence is 1.5 IQR above Q3.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_25_3"}
```r
iqr <- q[[2]] - q[[1]]
upper_fence <- q[[2]] + 1.5 * iqr
max(x[x <= upper_fence])
rownames(mtcars)[x > upper_fence]

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = "")) + geom_boxplot()
```
The upper fence is about 305.25 hp; the whisker ends at the largest car below it (264 hp) and only the Maserati Bora (335 hp) is flagged.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — compare distributions with an ECDF.** Draw the ECDFs of flipper length for the three penguin species. Use the plot to estimate the median flipper length of each species, then check with `summarise()`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_25_4
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, colour = ______)) +
  ______(na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Proportion ≤ x")

penguins |>
  summarise(median = median(flipper_len, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_25_4"}
Map `colour = species` and use `stat_ecdf()`. The median is where each curve crosses the dashed line.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_25_4"}
```r
ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, colour = species)) +
  stat_ecdf(na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Proportion ≤ x")
```
The curves cross 0.5 at about 190 mm (Adelie), 196 mm (Chinstrap) and 216 mm (Gentoo), matching the medians from `summarise()`. The Gentoo curve lies entirely to the right: nearly every Gentoo has longer flippers than nearly every Adelie.
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — four views of one variable.** For `bill_len` in `penguins` by species, draw (a) overlaid densities, (b) violins with boxplots, (c) boxplots with jittered points, (d) ECDFs. Write two sentences on what each plot shows best.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
p <- ggplot(penguins, aes(colour = species, fill = species))

p + geom_density(aes(bill_len), alpha = 0.3, na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(penguins, aes(species, bill_len)) +
  geom_violin(na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, outlier.shape = NA, na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(penguins, aes(species, bill_len)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.4, na.rm = TRUE)

p + stat_ecdf(aes(bill_len), na.rm = TRUE)
```
Adelie penguins have clearly shorter bills; Chinstrap and Gentoo overlap a lot (Chinstrap slightly longer on average). Densities and violins show the shapes, jittered points show the actual data and group sizes, and the ECDF makes it easy to read proportions and medians.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Plot | ggplot2 | Shows best |
|---|---|---|
| Histogram | `geom_histogram(binwidth = , boundary = )` | Shape, modes, gaps |
| Density | `geom_density(adjust = )` | Smooth shape; overlaid groups |
| Boxplot | `geom_boxplot()`; `notch = TRUE` | Median, IQR, outliers; many groups |
| Jittered points | `geom_jitter(width = , height = 0)` | Every observation, group size |
| Dot plot | `geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center")` | Every observation, stacked |
| Violin | `geom_violin()` | Shape per group |
| ECDF | `stat_ecdf()` | Proportions ≤ x, quantiles, whole-distribution comparison |
| Group summary | `stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point")` | Adding a mean to a plot |

- **Look at the distribution**, not just a summary: means can sit where no data are.
- Bin width and bandwidth are **choices**; try several.
- Boxplot whiskers reach the most extreme point within **1.5 × IQR**; points beyond are *potential* outliers.
- Non-overlapping **notches** suggest different medians; overlap proves nothing.
- With few observations, **show the points**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
